title: We Have a Tier 0 Problem
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart presents Play Deprivation Delay Theory: the claim that rising meltdowns, executive function delays and behavior referrals reflect lost free play rather than worse children, parents or teachers. Using the MTSS pyramid, he argues that systems omit a foundation layer, which he names Tier 0, the unstructured play, independence and responsibility that childhood used to supply. Drawing on Vygotsky, Peter Gray and Stuart Brown, he explains how deprived children arrive at school with fewer practice reps in waiting, losing and repairing conflict. He maintains that adding programs at higher tiers answers a Tier 0 problem with the wrong tool and that SEL lessons cannot substitute for lived experience. He closes with a reframing question, what chances has this child had to practice this, and a call to give play back.
points: Behavior crises may be developmental delays caused by lost play, so labeling noncompliance or disorder misreads the cause.
Tiered support systems assume a foundation of play-built self-regulation that many children no longer have, overloading Tier 2 and 3 teams.
Self-regulation grows through real, edge-of-ability experiences, so explicit SEL teaching alone cannot replace play.
Stinehart replaces what is wrong with this kid with a practice-based question about where the child has rehearsed waiting, losing and sharing.
The remedy is to restore daily inputs such as free play, independence, responsibility and boredom rather than add programs.
quotes: We have quietly dismantled the developmental conditions childhood used to provide automatically, and now we are living with the effects. That’s all Play Deprivation Delay Theory (PDDT) really is.

First, we deprive kids of the kind of play that builds their brains and bodies. Then, we label and punish them for the delays that deprivation created. Finally, we blame the child, the parent, or the teacher instead of the conditions.

In other words: play (real, messy, kid-led play) is supposed to be the primary classroom for everything we now call “self-regulation,” “executive function,” and “social-emotional skills.” Our school systems were built assuming that classroom was still open and giving kids the crucial primary education they’ll need for school and beyond.

So a five-year-old who cannot wait more than five seconds without erupting? That’s not a “bad five-year-old.” That’s a nervous system that has had very few reps at not getting what it wants immediately.
And that’s why so many educators tell me their systems feel like they’re always bailing water out of a sinking boat. The leak is not in the tiers and supports. The leak is in the hull of the boat.
It means we stop expecting a sturdy house where we’ve removed the foundation. It means we stop calling it a behavior epidemic when, it’s a play epidemic.
